topic: What the Bloop, the loud mystery sound in the Pacific, really was
hook: The ocean made a sound nobody could explain.

scenes.narration: In 1997, researchers were listening for underwater volcanic activity in the southern Pacific when their hydrophones picked up something enormous.
scenes.on_screen_text: 1997: a sound in the southern Pacific

scenes.narration: Underwater microphones placed more than 3,219 kilometres apart caught it. It was so loud and so strange that it earned its own name: the Bloop.
The guesses poured in. Secret military tests. Ship engines. Whales. A giant squid. Maybe a sea creature nobody had ever seen.
But the real answer is stranger than a monster, and it took years to find.
Scientists at NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory did not give up. They kept moving their hydrophones closer and closer to Antarctica, following the sound south.
In 2005, they finally tracked it down. The Bloop was an icequake: an iceberg cracking and breaking away from an Antarctic glacier.
No monster at all. No secret weapon either. Just ice, splitting with enough force to be heard across the Pacific. And about 95 percent of the ocean is still unexplored.

loop_line: So the next time the ocean makes a sound nobody can explain, do not picture a monster. Listen for the ice.
title: The Bloop: the ocean's mystery sound, solved
description: Source: What is the Bloop? NOAA National Ocean Service, Ocean Facts. https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/bloop.html
